ety.text: From Middle English rust, rost, roust, from Old English rust, rūst (“rust”), from Proto-West Germanic *rust, from Proto-Germanic *rustaz (“rust”), from Proto-Indo-European *rudʰso- (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Cognate with Scots roust (“rust”), Saterland Frisian rust (“rust”), West Frisian roast (“rust”), Dutch roest (“rust”), German Rost (“rust”), Danish rust (“rust”), Swedish rost (“rust”), Norwegian rust, ryst (“rust”), Finnish ruoste, Estonian rooste. Related to red.
From Middle English rusten, from the noun (see above).

senses.d: The deteriorated state of iron or steel as a result of moisture and oxidation; it consists mostly of iron(III) oxide (ferric oxide) and iron(II) oxide (ferrous oxide).
ex: The rust on my bicycle chain made cycling to work very dangerous.

senses.d: A similar substance based on another metal.
ex: copper rust

senses.d: A reddish-brown color.
A disease of plants caused by a reddish-brown fungus (Pucciniales).
Damage caused to stamps and album pages by a fungal infection.
To oxidize, especially of iron or steel.
ex: The patio furniture had rusted in the wind-driven spray.
Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire.

senses.d: To cause to oxidize.
ex: The wind-driven spray had thoroughly rusted the patio furniture.

senses.d: To be affected with the parasitic fungus called rust.
ex: I am sorry to say that, contrary to the majority, I have to report that the forage rusted rather badly.

senses.d: To (cause to) degenerate in idleness; to make or become dull or impaired by inaction.
ex: My knowledge of Spanish has rusted over the years.
Must I rust in Egypt? never more / Appear in arms, and be the chief of Greece?

senses.d: Of a black cat or its fur, to turn rust-coloured following long periods of exposure to sunlight.
ex: It's very common for black cats to rust during the summer.

fr:rouille.gl: rust (oxidation of iron or, by extension, other metals)

ety.text: Inherited from Old French reoïlle, from Vulgar Latin *robicla, from syncopation of Latin *robicula, a diminutive of Latin rōbīgō (“rust”) + -cula (from -culus (suffix forming diminutives)). Rōbīgō is derived from rōbus (a variant of rūfus (“red, reddish”)) + -īgō (suffix forming nouns usually denoting diseased conditio…
Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin acidusbor. French acide blend French oxydebor. Spanish óxido Borrowed from French oxyde.
Unknown, but proposed possibilities include: * Of expressive origin. * A Germanic borrowing, from Old High German *muff (“mold”) or a similar source. Compare Portuguese mofo and Italian muffa.

chain.g: rust (or the colour), specifically iron-rust or its colour

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese ferrugen, from Latin ferrūginem.
Borrowed from Aragonese roya, feminine of royo, from Latin rubeus. Doublet of rubio.
First attested in Old French. From rouille + -er.
Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Italic *-iðos Latin -idus Latin acidusbor. French acide blend French oxydebor. Portuguese óxido Portuguese -ar Portuguese oxidar From óxido + -ar.

From Middle English rusty, from Old English rūstiġ (“rusty”), from Proto-Germanic *rustagaz (“rusty”), equivalent to rust + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian rusterch (“rusty”), West Frisian rustich, roastich (“rusty”), Dutch roestig (“rusty”), German Low German rusterig, rüsterig (“rusty”), German rostig (“rusty”), Swedish rostig (“rusty”).

Ellipsis of rusty one more often used for this, or from the general epithet rusty given to various particular firearm names—earlier both were applied in Cockney rhyming slang for other machines, including swords in their day, but the present coinage has not more than a loose connection to this and is from the preference for used or antique firearms due to their being easier or cheaper to obtain.
Variant form of resty; compare also reasty.

senses.d: Marked or corroded by rust.
Of the rust color, reddish or reddish-brown.
ex: Alive? he might be dead for aught I know, / With that red gaunt and colloped neck a-strain, / And shut eyes underneath the rusty mane;

senses.d: Lacking recent experience, out of practice, especially with respect to a skill or activity.
Of clothing, especially dark clothing: worn, shabby.
ex: He wore a black jacket, rusty and amorphous.
The clerk stared at him and the rusty black bonnet a moment, and then laughed.

senses.d: Affected with the fungal plant disease called rust.
A gun or in particular an old or worn one.
ex:
My angles dusty, two black hands on the rusty
And I got uck from a peng ting, mad back but the chest busty

senses.d: Discolored and rancid; reasty.
ex: rusty bacon

senses.d: Cantankerous
ex: But they paraded the street, and watched the yard till dusk, when its proprietor ran rusty and turned them out.

grp.label: of the rust color, reddish or reddish-brown
lacking recent experience, out of practice

phr: better than a poke in the eye with a rusty nail

ety.text: Perhaps from Middle English ruschen, russchen (“to rush, startle, make a loud rushing noise”), from Old English hrysċan (“to jolt, startle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hurskijan, from Proto-Germanic *hurskijaną (“to startle, drive”), from *hurskaz (“fast, rapid, quick”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run, hurry”). Cognate with Old High German hursken (“to hurry, speed, incite, accelerate”), Old English horsċ (“quick, quick-witted, clever”), Old Frisian rosk, rosch (“quick, rapid, sudden”).

From Middle English risshe, rusch, risch, from Old English rysċ, rysċe, risċ, risċe, from a merger of Proto-West Germanic *riskijā, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)resg- (“to weave”) and Proto-West Germanic *ruskijā, possibly borrowed from Latin rūscum (“butcher's broom”), of unknown origin + *-jā (animal and plant suffix). Cognates include West Frisian risk, Dutch rus (“bulrush”), Norwegian Bokmål rusk, dialectal Norwegian ryskje (“hair-grass”). Further cognates include Russian ро́зга (rózga).

senses.d: A sudden forward motion.
ex: A gentleman of his train spurred up his horse, and, with a violent rush, severed him from the duke.

senses.d: A surge.
ex: A rush of business can be difficult to handle effectively for its unexpected volume.

senses.d: General haste.
ex: Many errors were made in the rush to finish.

senses.d: A rapid, noisy flow.
ex: a rush of water; a rush of footsteps

senses.d: A sudden attack; an onslaught.
The strategy of attacking an opponent with a large swarm of weak units, rather than spending time developing their abilities.
The act of running at another player to block or disrupt play.
ex: a rush on the quarterback

senses.d: A rusher; a lineman.
ex: the center rush, whose place is in the center of the rush line

senses.d: A sudden, brief exhilaration, for instance the pleasurable sensation produced by a stimulant.
ex: The rollercoaster gave me a rush.
She felt the familiar cocaine rush soon after injecting herself.

senses.d: A regulated period of recruitment in fraternities and sororities.
ex: rush week

senses.d: To hurry; to perform a task with great haste, often not properly or without thinking carefully.
ex: rush one's dinner; rush off an email response

senses.d: To flow or move forward rapidly or noisily.
ex: armies rush to battle; waters rush down a precipice.
Like to an entred Tyde, they all ruſh by,[…]

senses.d: To dribble rapidly.
To run directly at another player in order to block or disrupt play.
To cause to move or act with unusual haste.
ex: Don't rush your client or he may withdraw.

senses.d: To make a swift or sudden attack.
To swiftly attack without warning.
ex: A detachment of cavalrymen rushed the enemy's position.

senses.d: To attack (an opponent) with a large swarm of units.
To transport or carry quickly.
ex: The shuttle rushes passengers from the station to the airport.

senses.d: To roquet an object ball to a particular location on the lawn.
Performed with, or requiring urgency or great haste, or done under pressure, especially if therefore done badly.
ex: a rush job

senses.d: Any of several stiff plants of the genus Juncus, or the family Juncaceae, having hollow or pithy stems and small flowers, and often growing in marshes or near water.
The stem of such plants used in making baskets, mats, the seats of chairs, etc.
The merest trifle; a straw.
A wick.

senses.d: Very busy.
ex: I was so rushed today, I didn't have time to eat lunch.

senses.d: Done in haste; done quickly or hastily.
ex: My rushed attempt at an essay received a predictably poor grade.

senses.d: Abounding or covered with rushes.
ex: […] once densely rushed, into a condition practically free from rushes.
